findings.issue: Rate-limiting is fail-open on Redis outage for BOTH the global /events limit and the per-subscriber auto-enroll limit. With Redis down, /events has NO throttle at all: an attacker holding a valid key (or, combined with the global limit being the only gate, any caller during the outage window) can flood the endpoint, each request fanning out N FunnelExecution inserts -> unbounded Mongo write + JobRunr enqueue amplification. The depth cap (10) bounds chain DEPTH but not request VOLUME, so it does not close this hole at the API ingress. The user-spec justifies fail-open as 'availability > hard limit during Redis outage', which is a reasonable stance for an internal counter, but for an unauthenticated-by-volume public ingress it converts a Redis blip into an application-layer DoS amplifier.
findings.recommendation: Keep fail-open semantics but add a Redis-independent ceiling at the ingress, mirroring the depth-cap philosophy: (a) a hard per-request fan-out cap (max active listener funnels dispatched per single /events call, e.g. <=50) enforced in FunnelEventService regardless of Redis, and/or (b) a coarse in-process token bucket / semaphore on the EventsController as a backstop when Redis is unreachable. Document the residual exposure explicitly in Decision 10. At minimum, state the maximum amplification factor (N listeners x rate) the design tolerates during a Redis outage.

findings.issue: API key strength, format, and lifecycle are underspecified at the design level. The spec says 'SecureRandom -> plaintext shown once' and 'Sha256Hex.hex(plaintext)' but does NOT pin: (1) key entropy/length (code-research suggests 32 bytes but the tech-spec Decision 8 / Data Models do not mandate it); (2) that the hash input is the FULL high-entropy key (SHA-256 with no salt/stretch is acceptable ONLY because the key is high-entropy random; if a short or low-entropy key were chosen, an offline brute-force of a leaked api_keys dump becomes feasible since unsalted SHA-256 is fast); (3) key expiry/rotation is explicitly deferred to Epic 08, so a leaked key is valid indefinitely with no TTL and the only remediation is manual Regenerate.
findings.recommendation: In Decision 8 / Data Models, mandate: minimum 256 bits (32 bytes) of SecureRandom entropy encoded URL-safe; assert the unsalted-SHA-256-at-rest choice is sound ONLY under that entropy floor (add a unit test asserting generated key length/charset). Note the no-expiry/no-rotation residual risk as an accepted, time-boxed limitation tied to Epic 08, and ensure the Regenerate path invalidates the old hash atomically (overwrite, single primary key per project -> confirmed, good).

findings.issue: Key-comparison timing is not explicitly specified. The design authenticates via lookup-by-hash (hash the presented key, then findByKeyHash on a unique Mongo index). This is effectively constant-time with respect to the SECRET because the comparison happens over a high-entropy 256-bit hash, not the plaintext, so per-character timing leakage of the secret is not exploitable. This is acceptable. However, the existing codebase establishes an explicit constant-time pattern (WebhookSecretVerifier uses MessageDigest.isEqual and forbids String.equals); the tech-spec's lookup-by-hash approach silently diverges from that convention without stating WHY it is safe, which invites an implementer to 'fix' it by adding a plaintext or non-constant-time compare.
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence to Decision 8: 'Authentication is lookup-by-hash on the unique keyHash index; no plaintext comparison occurs, so the WebhookSecretVerifier-style MessageDigest.isEqual is unnecessary here (the only equality is over a 256-bit hash via the DB index).' This prevents a well-meaning reviewer from forcing an unnecessary (or worse, non-constant-time) plaintext compare. Confirm the filter NEVER falls back to a String.equals on plaintext anywhere.

findings.issue: IDOR surface on subscriber resolution is correctly mitigated in principle (both telegram_user_id and subscriber_id are resolved as (projectId, identifier) where projectId is pinned FROM the key, not from the request body), so a key for project A cannot resolve a subscriber in project B. This is the right design. Residual concern: the spec must guarantee the projectId used in resolution is ALWAYS the key-derived one and that subscriber_id from the request body is NEVER used as a global lookup or trusted across the project boundary. The 404-vs-202 response split also leaks a cross-project existence oracle ONLY if resolution ignored projectId scoping -- it does not, given the design, but the implementation must not introduce a project-unscoped findById(subscriber_id) shortcut.
findings.recommendation: Make the project-scoping invariant explicit and testable: the integration test matrix should include 'key for project A + subscriber_id belonging to project B -> 404 (not 202, not data leak)'. Forbid any repository call of the form findById(subscriberId) without the projectId predicate in the api/dispatch path. Decision 7/8 should state 'projectId is taken exclusively from the authenticated key principal and is non-overridable by the request body.'

findings.issue: Anti-enumeration via uniform 401 is well covered for KEY problems, but the /events RESPONSE matrix itself (202 success / 202 no-op / 404 unknown subscriber) exposes a subscriber-existence oracle to any holder of a valid project key: 404 means 'this telegram_user_id/subscriber_id does not exist in MY project', 202 means it does. Within a single project boundary this is arguably acceptable (the key owner is entitled to know their own subscribers), and conflating 404 into 202 would harm the legitimate integrator's debuggability (the user-spec explicitly wants 404 for unknown subscriber). So this is an accepted trade-off rather than a flaw -- but it should be acknowledged, and the 404 body must be minimal (no subscriber data, no project metadata, no echo of the supplied id beyond what the caller already sent).
findings.recommendation: Accept the 404/202 split as in-project-scope-only (the oracle never crosses project boundaries because resolution is project-pinned -- see the IDOR finding). Specify that 202/404/429 bodies are static/minimal: no PII, no subscriber id echo, no funnel names, no count of matched funnels. Add this as an explicit acceptance criterion ('response bodies contain no subscriber or funnel data').

findings.issue: event_name is well-constrained (^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$). Two input-validation gaps remain at design level: (1) telegram_user_id is typed 'long' but the spec does not state bounds/positive-only validation; a negative or zero value should be rejected at the DTO boundary (Telegram user ids are positive), and an absent telegram_user_id WITH an absent subscriber_id must be a deterministic 400/404, not an NPE-driven 5xx (the 'never 5xx' guarantee depends on this). (2) subscriber_id is an optional opaque string used in a Mongo query; it must be treated as an exact-match equality value (not a regex/operator), and its length/charset should be bounded to avoid oversized-document or query-shape abuse. The contains-match keyword scan operates on author-curated lists (trusted), so no injection there.
findings.recommendation: Pin DTO-level validation: telegram_user_id positive long; require exactly one of (telegram_user_id, subscriber_id) present (or define precedence) and map the missing/both-absent case to a deterministic 400/404 before engine dispatch; bound subscriber_id length (e.g. <=64) and charset, and ensure it is bound as a value (Spring Data derived query / Criteria.is(), never a $where/regex). Confirm Bean Validation runs INSIDE the key chain so a malformed body returns 4xx, not 5xx.

findings.owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.issue: Logging discipline (ids/codes only, never payload/PII, greppable WARN markers) is inherited from the established conventions and is good. Two design-level gaps: (1) there is NO positive audit trail for the authentication EVENT on the public ingress -- the spec defines greppable WARNs for rate-limit DROPS and engine faults, but nothing records successful/failed key authentications, so credential-stuffing or a leaked-key abuse pattern against /api/integrations/** would be invisible. lastUsedAt is 'optional' in the data model. (2) The keyPrefix mask is shown in the UI; the spec must ensure the prefix is short enough that logging it (if ever logged for support) does not materially reduce key entropy.
findings.recommendation: Add a security-event log line (greppable, project-id + outcome only, NO key/hash) on key-auth failure at the filter, and on rate-limit 429, so abuse is detectable. Make lastUsedAt non-optional (cheap, aids leaked-key detection). Cap keyPrefix at a small fixed length (e.g. 6-8 chars of a 43-char base64 key) and state that the full key and full hash are NEVER logged, only the prefix and projectId.

findings.issue: CSRF-disabled on the @Order(1) /api/integrations/** chain is correctly justified (header-based key auth, no ambient cookie credential -> not CSRF-able). Chain mutual-exclusion is sound: securityMatcher('/api/integrations/**') on @Order(1) carves the namespace before the session chain's broad /api/** matcher, and the IT matrix proves key-does-not-auth-cabinet and session-does-not-auth-integrations. One residual: the key is presented in a request HEADER (X-API-Key / Authorization: Bearer per code-research) -- the design must forbid accepting the key via query string or cookie, otherwise it could land in access logs / browser history / Referer and defeat the hash-only-at-rest protection. Also, since CSRF is off on this chain, the chain must NOT also accept the session cookie as an alternate credential (it must not), or a CSRF hole reopens.
findings.recommendation: State explicitly: the key is accepted ONLY from a request header (never query param, never cookie); the @Order(1) chain authenticates SOLELY via the api-key filter and never falls through to session/cookie authentication (stateless, SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS on this chain). Keep the mutual-isolation ITs. Enforce HTTPS-only for the public endpoint in the deploy posture (key in cleartext header over HTTP is a sniffing risk) -- note this even though deploy is deferred.

summary: Architecture-level review of the 12-funnels-triggers tech-spec against OWASP Top 10. No HIGH/critical findings: the core security decisions are sound by design -- hash-only (SHA-256) API-key storage with plaintext-shown-once and SecureRandom generation; lookup-by-hash authentication that is effectively constant-time over a high-entropy hash (no plaintext compare); uniform 401 anti-enumeration on any key problem; a dedicated @Order(1) /api/integrations/** filter chain with mutual session-isolation and justified CSRF-disable (header-based, cookieless); project-scoped subscriber resolution that closes cross-project IDOR; a well-constrained event_name slug; and two independent loop backstops (Redis fail-open volume limit + Redis-independent depth cap). Eight lower-severity, mostly hardening findings: (medium) fail-open rate-limiting on a public ingress is a Redis-outage DoS-amplification hole that the depth cap does not close at the API layer -- add a Redis-independent per-request fan-out ceiling; (medium) key entropy/length and the no-rotation/no-expiry lifecycle are underspecified, and unsalted SHA-256 at rest is safe ONLY if a 256-bit key floor is mandated; (low) make the lookup-by-hash 'no plaintext compare, hence no MessageDigest.isEqual needed' rationale explicit so an implementer does not regress it; (low) make the project-scoping invariant on subscriber resolution explicit and testable (forbid project-unscoped findById); (low) keep but acknowledge the in-project 404/202 subscriber-existence oracle and mandate minimal/PII-free 202/404/429 bodies; (low) tighten telegram_user_id/subscriber_id DTO validation (positive long, exactly-one-of, bounded opaque value bound via Criteria.is not regex) to preserve the never-5xx guarantee; (low) add positive auth-event/abuse logging on the public ingress (key-auth failure, 429) and make lastUsedAt non-optional; (low) forbid key-in-query/cookie, pin STATELESS no-cookie-fallback on the key chain, and require HTTPS-only for the public endpoint. Verdict: design APPROVED with recommended hardening -- the two medium items (fail-open ingress ceiling, key entropy/lifecycle wording) should be folded into Decisions 8 and 10 before implementation; the rest are implementation-time guardrails to encode as acceptance criteria for the Wave-3 tasks and the Task-14 code-level security audit.
